summary:
Canarias stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 1 March 2023, which applies uniformly across all autonomous communities. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may rectify the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry by simple declaration, with no prior medical diagnosis or gender-dysphoria finding and no requirement of two years of medical treatment; corresponding identity documents are adapted to the new marker. The law also mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and consent for medical procedures is regulated for minors aged 12 to 16. That provision proved contentious in the Congress of Deputies, which passed the law on 16 February 2023. Human Rights Watch placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Canarias rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the Civil Registry is the operative basis for facility rules. A trans visitor whose documents reflect a corrected marker is therefore treated on that basis in practice.

The regional layer is permissive rather than restrictive. Canarias enacted Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising trans persons' rights, and has permitted self-declaration of legal gender since 2021, one of 14 autonomous communities to do so before the national law took effect. The region is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and it created its same-sex couple registry in 2003.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice, though the documented cases come from outside Canarias. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied across Spain since 2005, and Ley 4/2023 enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples. Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations.
tangentialFactors:
The national law also expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, and bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent. None of these bear directly on a visitor's entry, documents or movement, but they indicate the direction of the surrounding legal regime.

Canarias is not an outlier within Spain. The regional anti-discrimination statute of 2014 and the self-declaration route available from 2021 predate the national law, so the 2023 framework layers onto an existing permissive base rather than replacing a restrictive one. The dedicated country dossier identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately.

Enforcement evidence for the transphobia aggravation is drawn from mainland jurisdictions. A visitor to Canarias should read the Vigo and Valencia outcomes as proof that the aggravation is being invoked and sentenced on, not as a description of Canarian courts.

Gran Canaria and Tenerife carry an established international LGBT tourism profile, which generally correlates with visible venues and a higher tolerance threshold in tourist zones, while offering no guarantee of protection elsewhere on the islands.

The regional conversion-therapy ban is stated as a listing among communities that prohibit the practice; the enabling statute, its date and its penalties are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved.
